strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: embedding synthesis constraints directly into GA operators (crossover, Grow, Shrink, Rerun, Change internal/leaf) so that every generated molecule is valid and synthesizable by construction, avoiding the training cost and generalization issues of projection models like SynNet or SynFormer.
Unified framework that handles both analog search and property optimization with only a fitness-function change, including 3D (docking) objectives — a broad demonstration scope.

Strong, extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ChEMBL analog search, projection of structure-based/goal-directed designs, full PMO suite, LIT-PCBA docking), with appropriate and up-to-date baselines (SynNet, SynthesisNet, ChemProjector, SynFormer, GPBO, f-RAG, Genetic GFN, SynFlowNet, RxnFlow, 3DSynthFlow).

SynGBO achieves state-of-the-art among synthesis-aware methods on PMO (16.426, exceeding even unconstrained GPBO/f-RAG) and best docking scores on LIT-PCBA with 4x fewer oracle calls than GFlowNet baselines.

Excellent ablation studies: filter choices (Table 1), GA vs. random search under filtering (Table 7), mutation operator weights (Table 6), NAM ranking vs. MSE loss (Table 9), NAM+GP synergy (Table 8), and honest hard-negative-mining negative results.
Impressive lightweight design: MLP filter (~1.8M params) and NAM (~140k params) provide large gains; SynGA is ML-free and parallelizable, making it a useful standalone baseline and composable module.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (runtime 3x slower than SynFormer, template-based caveats, single-objective scope, runtime benchmarking caveats) and a solid reproducibility statement with promised code and model checkpoints.
Careful handling of benchmark subtleties (PyTDC version discrepancies, Valsartan SMARTS pathology, query clustering, edge cases in genetic operators).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: GAs over synthesis routes have been explored before (SYNOPSIS, ChemProjector-style projections, MolGA-style operators), so the contribution is primarily well-engineered genetic operators plus block filtering rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

PMO results are obtained on a modified benchmark (Valsartan SMARTS removed, PyTDC 1.1.14 instead of the original 0.3.6), and baseline numbers are imported from other papers evaluated under different conditions; while the changes are justified, this weakens the strictness of 'state-of-the-art' claims versus prior reported numbers.

Some comparisons have budget/hardware confounds: docking baselines use 64k oracle calls vs. 16k for SynGA/SynGBO; runtime comparisons with SynFormer acknowledge substantial limitations (different worker counts, non-optimized codebases); SynGBO runs ~100x more SynGA iterations than standalone SynGA, making the compute-for-quality tradeoff across variants hard to compare directly.

The analog-search classifier filter is trained on ~10M randomly sampled synthesis routes, a nontrivial upfront data-generation cost that is not fully accounted for when positioning SynGA as 'lightweight'.

Fairness concerns in Table 2: baselines use different building-block catalogs (147k vs 223k) and template sets (91 vs 115 incl. trimolecular), so the head-to-head similarity comparisons are approximate rather than controlled.
Baseline seed counts vary (3 and 1 seeds for some baselines in Table 4), limiting statistical rigor of some comparisons.
Sensitivity of results to the epsilon-filtering and mutation-probability hyperparameters is only partially explored; the mutation ablation is limited to two PMO tasks.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: embedding synthesis constraints directly into the genetic operators (crossover over compatible subtrees, five tree-based mutations) so that every individual is a valid synthesis route by construction, avoiding the training/inference costs and generalization risks of learned projection modules (SynNet, ChemProjector, SynFormer).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple problem types: synthesizable analog search (ChEMBL tasks), projection of structure-based and goal-directed designs (Table 3), the PMO benchmark (22 tasks, 5 seeds, task-wise results in appendix), and 3D docking on LIT-PCBA with quarter the oracle calls of baselines.

Honest and useful ablations: filter variants (Sim/MLP/MLP+Mine, Table 1), SynGA vs. random search over filtered blocks (Table 7), NAM vs. GP vs. coupled models (Table 8), mutation operator weights (Table 6), MSE vs. ranking loss (Table 9), and runtime benchmarking with acknowledged limitations (Appendix B.4).

The ML augmentations are pragmatic and well-integrated: fingerprint-MLP block filtering for analog search and NAM+GP building block filtering inside a BO loop (SynGBO) yield clear gains, with SynGBO reaching SOTA-level PMO and docking results among synthesis-aware (and competitive with unconstrained) methods.

Solid positioning against prior work, explicit limitations section, reproducibility statement with hardware/compute details, and promised code release. Careful handling of benchmarking pitfalls (PyTDC versioning, removing the ill-posed Valsartan SMARTS task with justification).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Genetic algorithms operating over synthesis routes/building blocks have a long history (SYNOPSIS, Button et al., ChemistGA, MolGA plus projection models), and the individual components — fingerprint MLP filters, NAMs, GP-based BO, elitist selection, inverse-rank sampling — are all standard. The contribution is largely a careful engineering combination of known pieces, which may limit impact for a top-tier venue.

Headline claims of state-of-the-art require qualifications: SynGA alone trails the best synthesis-agnostic methods on PMO (13.4 vs ~16.3), and the SynGBO SOTA depends on the inner-loop configuration (100x more SynGA iterations), block filtering, and GPBO machinery largely inherited from Tripp & Hernández-Lobato. Comparisons across baselines use different building block catalogs (147k/196k/223k blocks), template sets (91 vs 115 reactions), and seed counts (1 seed for SynthesisNet), so the comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples.

Several evaluation choices weaken rigor: fitness function (0.9·Morgan + 0.1·Murcko) directly optimized for the evaluation metrics on the ChEMBL analog task; arbitrary subset of three LIT-PCBA receptors; removal of a PMO task; runtime comparisons described as 'rough estimates' with unequal worker allocations; similarity-based query clustering that reduces effective sample sizes in Table 3.

SynGBO shows reduced diversity relative to SynGA (Table 15: 0.388 vs 0.514), and diversity is a key practical concern in molecular design that is under-discussed given how heavily the top modes appear optimized.

Some design decisions lack justification or external validation: mutation probabilities fixed without principled rationale (only a small two-task sensitivity study), ε=0.1 filtering set ad hoc, NAM additivity assumption acknowledged as a limitation but only probed on two oracles, and no wet-lab or retrosynthesis-model validation of the 'synthesizability' of proposed routes beyond template matching.
Runtime disadvantage (3x slower than SynFormer in Table 2) and the reliance on a 64-core machine for parallelization limit the practical appeal of the lightweight claim in some settings.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: directly embedding synthesis constraints into a GA via custom crossover/mutation operators over synthesis trees, avoiding the training and inference costs of projection models (SynNet, ChemProjector, SynFormer) while guaranteeing valid routes by construction.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple problem classes: synthesizable analog search (ChEMBL 100 and 1k tasks), projection of structure-based and goal-directed designs (LIT-PCBA, GuacaMol), the full PMO suite (22 tasks, 5 seeds), and 3D docking objectives, with both 2D and 3D objectives covered.

The ML augmentation (block filtering via a simple MLP classifier for analog search, and NAM-based block filtering coupled with a GP in SynGBO for property optimization) is well-designed, lightweight, and clearly improves over the standalone GA; ablations (Tables 1, 6, 7, 8, 9) carefully isolate the contributions of the filter, the GA, the ranking loss, and mutation operators.

State-of-the-art results are convincingly supported: SynGBO exceeds synthesis-agnostic baselines on PMO (16.426 vs. 16.304 for GPBO) and achieves the best docking scores among synthesis-aware methods with a quarter of the oracle calls.

Unusually honest and thorough limitations discussion: runtime caveats (Appendix B.4), the non-guarantee of synthesizability by templates, single-objective scope, PyTDC versioning issues, and justification for removing Valsartan SMARTS are all transparently reported.
Strong reproducibility: detailed pseudocode (Algorithms 1 and 2), hyperparameters, compute/hardware details, code release, and planned checkpoint release.
The inverse-rank sampling analysis (Appendix A.3) connecting their selection scheme to MolGA's quantile-based sampling is a nice touch of rigor.
The paper positions itself well as both a strong standalone baseline and a modular component for future synthesis-aware workflows.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core method is a straightforward application of GA machinery to a template-based synthesis-tree representation; similar synthesis-constrained evolutionary approaches exist (SYNOPSIS, ChemistGA, SynNet+GA hybrids), so the primary novelty lies in operator design and empirical strength rather than a fundamentally new idea.

SynGA alone (13.366 on PMO) still trails synthesis-agnostic baselines substantially; the SOTA claim rests entirely on the augmented SynGBO variant, which relies on external ML components (GP, NAM), weakening the claim that the GA itself is the driver of the improvement.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: SynNet/SynthesisNet use different building-block catalogs (147k vs. 197k) and SynFormer uses a different reaction set (115 templates incl. trimolecular) and block set (223k), so some head-to-head comparisons conflate method and search-space differences.
A PMO task (Valsartan SMARTS) is removed based on the authors' own argument; while justified, deviating from the standard benchmark protocol complicates comparability with published results.
SynGBO shows reduced diversity relative to SynGA (0.388 vs. 0.514 top-10 diversity in Table 15), which is not discussed in depth despite diversity being a common concern in molecular design.

Runtime comparisons are acknowledged as rough estimates with methodological limitations (single environment, non-optimized codebases), and SynGA is 3x slower than SynFormer at inference, which somewhat undercuts the 'lightweight' framing for analog search.
All evidence is computational; there is no wet-lab or retrosynthesis-model validation that the proposed routes are practically feasible, which is the ultimate claim motivating the work.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated idea: embedding synthesis constraints directly into GA crossover/mutation operators over synthesis trees, avoiding costly ML projection modules and guaranteeing valid routes by construction.

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct problem classes (synthesizable analog search, PMO property optimization, 3D docking), with appropriate and extensive baselines (SynNet, ChemProjector, SynFormer, SynthesisNet, GFlowNet variants, MolGA/GPBO, f-RAG, REINVENT) and strong reported results, including state-of-the-art SynGBO on PMO and competitive docking with 4x fewer oracle calls.

Unusually honest and thorough analysis: the authors report unfavorable comparisons (SynGA lags synthesis-agnostic methods on PMO, SynFormer outperforms on DDS-10/ZINC, SynGA is ~3x slower than SynFormer), include budget-tied runtime experiments, ablations for mutation operators, NAM loss, block filters, and search-space matching against 3DSynthFlow.

The ML augmentations (block filtering MLP, NAM-based filtering within Bayesian optimization) are elegant, lightweight, and clearly ablated (Tables 1, 7, 10, 11); the synergy between components is empirically demonstrated.

Good reproducibility posture: pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2), hyperparameters, hardware details, dataset preprocessing, and released code; appendix carefully documents benchmarking pitfalls (PyTDC versioning, Valsartan SMARTS removal with justification).
weaknesses: Core algorithmic novelty is moderate: the contribution is primarily careful engineering of genetic operators over synthesis trees plus known components (GPs, NAMs, UCB acquisition); experienced readers may view SynGA as a competent but not conceptually groundbreaking design.

Some experimental comparability concerns: comparisons against baselines rely partly on numbers copied from other papers run under different settings (different block catalogs, template sets, oracle call budgets, PyTDC versions); removing the Valsartan SMARTS task, while justified, further weakens direct comparability with published PMO numbers.

Runtime benchmarking is admittedly rough (single environment, non-optimized codebases, worker count differences between SynGA and SynFormer), so the 3x slowdown claim is imprecise; wall-clock efficiency claims should be taken cautiously.

Base SynGA underperforms synthesis-agnostic methods on PMO and SynFormer on most analog-search datasets; the headline 'state-of-the-art' claims hold only for the augmented SynGBO and specific synthesis-aware subsets, and the abstract/intro slightly overstate the generality of the result.

Several evaluation details are relegated to appendices with nontrivial tuning (e.g., offspring/population changes for docking, block-space matching ablation marked 'preliminary'), and the NAM additivity assumption's applicability to harder, non-additive objectives is only partially explored.

strengths: The core idea of enforcing synthesizability by construction via custom crossover/mutation operators over synthesis trees is clean and well-motivated; validity is guaranteed by design rather than via post-hoc projection, which is a genuine practical advantage.

Extensive and broad empirical evaluation across analog search (ChEMBL, DDS-10, ZINC), PMO property optimization, and LIT-PCBA docking, with task-wise results, seed counts, and multiple ablations (filters, mutation operators, ranking vs. MSE loss, budget tying) provided in the appendix.

Honest self-assessment in several places: the authors acknowledge slower runtime than SynFormer, that SynFormer outperforms SynGA on DDS-10/ZINC and in-distribution queries, and that SynGA alone lags synthesis-agnostic methods on PMO.

The building block filtering component (MLP classifier for analog search; NAM with ranking loss for property optimization) is simple, interpretable, and ablated against sensible alternatives, including a random-search control (Table 7).
Reproducibility materials appear thorough: hardware specs, hyperparameters, PyTDC versioning caveats, and pseudocode for both algorithms are provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: GAs that operate directly over template-based synthesis routes with custom operators have a long history (SYNOPSIS, Button et al. 2019, ChemistGA), and SynGBO is essentially GPBO with SynGA as the inner-loop optimizer plus a block filter. The contribution reads as careful engineering of known components rather than a new methodological idea.

Potentially unfair baseline comparisons: PMO results are reported after removing the Valsartan SMARTS task and using PyTDC 1.1.14 while baseline numbers are taken from other papers computed under different PyTDC versions and setups; docking baselines use 64k oracle calls versus 16k for SynGA/SynGBO, and the fitness function (QED-averaged Vina) differs from the baselines' protocol. These deviations, while individually justified, collectively undermine direct comparability of the claimed state-of-the-art results.

SynGA alone is not state-of-the-art on the main property optimization benchmark (13.366 vs. 16.30 for GPBO/f-RAG on PMO); the headline claim rests on SynGBO, which inherits most of its power from the Bayesian optimization machinery rather than from the proposed genetic operators.

Efficiency concerns: SynGA is over 3x slower than SynFormer at inference (250m vs. 80m), and SynGBO requires roughly 100x more SynGA iterations; the claimed 'lightweight' advantage is not clearly realized in practice, and the runtime analysis is admittedly rough.

The code availability link in the abstract and the 'Code' entry in Appendix E are empty placeholders in this submission, which is a serious reproducibility lapse for a paper whose central selling point is being a reusable baseline/module.

The MLP block filter is trained on 10M sampled synthesis routes, which is a substantial (though one-time) computational cost that sits somewhat in tension with the 'ML-free / lightweight' framing, and the generalization of this filter to out-of-distribution queries is only partially characterized (cf. the negative-mining results in B.3).

Generalization of hyperparameters (mutation weights, filtering thresholds, population sizes) is evaluated on only two PMO tasks; the authors themselves concede the ablation may not transfer, yet these settings are used across all benchmarks.

Missing synthesis realism: templates do not account for stereochemistry, conditions, yield, or cost (acknowledged in Appendix D), so 'state-of-the-art synthesizable molecular design' claims should be tempered; no comparison against the simplest synthesis-aware ablation of simply running an unconstrained GA on the enumerated product space is given for the docking task.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: directly embedding synthesis constraints into the genetic operators of a GA over synthesis trees, yielding guaranteed-valid routes without the training/inference overhead of projection models (SynNet, ChemProjector, SynFormer).

Strong and unusually thorough empirical evaluation spanning analog search (ChEMBL, DDS-10, ZINC), projection of ML-designed molecules, the full PMO benchmark, and 3D docking on LIT-PCBA, with task-wise results, multiple seeds, and honest reporting of where baselines win (e.g., SynFormer on DDS-10/ZINC, 3DSynthFlow on diversity).

The ML-augmented variants are well-designed and well-ablated: block filtering ablations (None/Sim/MLP/+Mine, Table 1), random-search control isolating GA vs. filter contributions (Table 7), NAM/GP/NAM+GP ablations (Table 10), ranking-vs-MSE loss (Table 11), mutation operator ablations (Table 6), and budget-tied runtime comparison (Table 8).

Notable attention to fairness and reproducibility details: PyTDC version pinning and the Valsartan SMARTS removal are well-justified, search-space ablations matching 3DSynthFlow (Table 13), runtime benchmarking with acknowledged limitations, hardware specs, and released code.

SynGBO achieves state-of-the-art among synthesis-aware methods on PMO and competitive/best docking scores using 4x fewer oracle calls than baselines, supporting the claim that SynGA is both a strong standalone baseline and a useful module.
The paper is candid about limitations (template-based constraints, single-objective scope, runtime vs. amortized models) and provides a thoughtful extended outlook.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest: evolutionary algorithms over template-based synthesis routes exist (SYNOPSIS, Button et al., ChemistGA, and GA+projection hybrids like SynNet), so the contribution is primarily a careful re-design of genetic operators plus existing BO wrapping (GPBO-style), rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The headline SOTA claims rest on SynGBO, whose gains largely come from the known GPBO-style acquisition wrapper rather than SynGA alone; standalone SynGA still trails synthesis-agnostic methods on PMO (13.4 vs ~16.3) and the SOTA framing could be considered slightly overclaimed.

Cross-method comparisons are imperfect: baselines use different building block catalogs, reaction template sets (91 vs 115), and oracle call budgets (16k vs 64k docking calls), and many numbers are imported from other papers under potentially differing conditions; the authors acknowledge but do not fully resolve this.

The analog-search task evaluates fitness directly on the evaluation metrics (0.9 Morgan + 0.1 Murcko), which is a form of training on the test metric and may inflate relative performance versus methods not optimized for those exact metrics; RR on 'reachable' datasets is notably worse than SynFormer.

Computational cost is non-trivial in practice: SynGA is ~3x slower than SynFormer on analog search and SynGBO runs SynGA ~100x more iterations internally; wall-clock practicality for larger catalogs (~200k blocks, precomputed substructure caches) may not scale, as the authors themselves note.

Some important details are deferred to the appendix, and a few experimental choices (mutation weights, epsilon=0.1, filter thresholds) are fixed without broad sensitivity analysis beyond the two-task ablation.
